claims.text: Thermal processing can induce a secondary precipitate phase in a high-entropy alloy.
The induced precipitates can be uniformly dispersed or concentrated at grain boundaries.
An HCP phase is a plausible thermally induced second phase in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
A ZrHf-rich phase is a plausible second phase in the proposed coating.
Dynamic precipitates can form along grain boundaries during high-stress creep of an FCC high-entropy alloy.
The precipitates restrict dislocation climb and glide during creep.
Restricting dislocation motion increases the effective stress required for plastic deformation.
Thermally processed coatings containing controlled precipitates will have a lower steady-state creep rate than a precipitate-suppressed baseline.
Thermally processed coatings containing controlled precipitates will have a longer creep time-to-failure than the baseline.
Processing that induces an HCP secondary phase can be accompanied by increased microhardness.
The precipitate-containing coating will show reduced dislocation mobility after creep testing.
Rapid cooling suppresses precipitation and produces a more homogeneous single-phase baseline.
The mechanism operates at elevated temperatures where diffusion-controlled dislocation climb and glide are active.
The mechanism ceases to be effective at temperatures that cause grain-boundary decohesion.
The mechanism ceases to be effective if the precipitates dissolve completely.
A controlled comparison between precipitate-inducing thermal treatment and rapid quenching can test the proposed mechanism.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or improved mechanical performance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies dynamic precipitation during loading as the governing factor, whereas the intervention and comparison primarily create different precipitate populations before loading. The design therefore does not cleanly distinguish dynamic precipitation from conventional hardening by pre-existing precipitates.

The falsification rule allows failure to generate a higher density of effective precipitates to reject the mechanism, but that outcome would represent a failed intervention rather than a decisive test of whether successfully generated precipitates improve creep resistance.
